spamInfo.whyDesc: reCAPTCHA and similar services send data about visitors to third parties, usually Google. That is questionable from a privacy standpoint, makes the site depend on a vendor, and locks some people out, for example those who cannot solve image puzzles. So the spam protection here runs entirely on this site's own server.
spamInfo.layer1Desc: Bots that blindly fill in every form field give themselves away. Humans never notice.
spamInfo.layer2Desc: If a submission arrives suspiciously soon after the page loaded, the server rejects it.
spamInfo.layer3Desc: The math question comes with an HMAC-signed token. The server checks both the answer and the token, without needing sessions or cookies.
spamInfo.layer4Desc: Only a few submissions per hour are accepted from any one IP address.
spamInfo.hmacDesc: The server signs the token with a secret key (HMAC-SHA256). Without that key nobody can produce a valid token, so it cannot be forged in the browser. Validation only happens on the server.

verifier.metaDescription: Verify the ML-DSA-65 signatures on this blog's articles and its cryptographic inventory.
verifier.label: // signature verification
verifier.description: Every article on this blog is signed with ML-DSA-65 (NIST FIPS 204). You can check any signature yourself here. All you need is the public key and the article data.
verifier.intro: A signature records what an article looked like when it was published. If someone changes the text later, for example directly in the database, the signature no longer matches and verification fails. ML-DSA-65 is considered secure against quantum computers, so the signatures stay meaningful once such machines exist. Verification runs entirely in your browser.
verifier.descriptionCbom: The cryptographic inventory (CBOM) is signed with ML-DSA-65 (NIST FIPS 204) as well. Here you can check that the CBOM you are looking at is exactly the one that was signed after the last scan.
verifier.introCbom: After every ShorSight scan, a script writes cbom.json and signs its exact UTF-8 content with the same private key that signs the articles. The signature sits next to it as cbom.sig. To verify, your browser fetches both files from this server and runs ML-DSA-65 locally.
verifier.messageFormatDesc: The four fields are joined with | and passed as UTF-8 bytes straight to ML-DSA-65, without hashing them first. ML-DSA processes the message internally with SHAKE-256 (FIPS 204, section 5.2). Media files are embedded in the blocks as SHA-256 hashes. The verifier fetches the title and blocks from Strapi itself, so you only need to enter the document ID.
verifier.messageFormatDescCbom: The signed message is the exact UTF-8 byte sequence of cbom.json (JSON.stringify with two-space indentation and a trailing newline). Nothing is added and nothing is left out: you are verifying exactly the file served at /cbom.json.
verifier.resultValid: Signature valid — content matches the signature.
verifier.resultInvalid: Signature invalid — content may have been modified.
verifier.resultError: Verification failed — public key missing or input invalid.
verifier.cbomResultValid: Signature valid — CBOM is authentic and unmodified.
verifier.cbomResultInvalid: Signature invalid — CBOM may have been tampered with.

playground.metaDescription: Interactive browser playground for hybrid post-quantum encryption: X25519 with ML-KEM-1024, Classic McEliece or FrodoKEM, plus AES-256-GCM. With tamper mode, KEM race, 20× benchmark and attacker view. Everything runs locally, no backend.
playground.label: // hybrid encryption
playground.title: Hybrid Encryption Playground
playground.intro: This playground walks through hybrid post-quantum encryption step by step. All computation happens in your browser. Pick a KEM (ML-KEM-1024, Classic McEliece or FrodoKEM), enter a message and click "Generate". X25519 (ECDH) and the chosen KEM each produce a shared secret, and HKDF-SHA-256 derives an AES-256-GCM key from both. Every value is marked as either transmitted or private. Afterwards you can change individual bytes in tamper mode and see where the protocol breaks, switch on the attacker's or a quantum computer's view, race all three KEMs against each other, or run a 20-round benchmark with statistics.
playground.mcElieceWarning: Note: Classic McEliece key generation is very compute-heavy and takes 10 to 30 seconds.
playground.mcElieceGeneratingNote: Depending on your device this takes 10 to 30 seconds. The page has not frozen, McEliece key generation is just expensive.
playground.step1Desc: Both sides generate their key pairs independently. Each private key stays with its owner.
playground.step2Desc: Elliptic-curve cryptography: client and server each multiply their private key by the other side's public key and arrive at the same result. A large enough quantum computer could break this step with Shor's algorithm.
playground.step3Desc: Lattice-based scheme from NIST FIPS 203, derived from Kyber-1024. Unlike Diffie-Hellman, the client encapsulates a random secret under the server's public key. Only the server can decapsulate it with its private key. ML-KEM-1024 is the strongest variant and reaches security category 5 (comparable to AES-256).
playground.step3DescMcEliece: Code-based scheme using binary Goppa codes, introduced by Robert McEliece in 1978. That makes it one of the oldest public-key schemes there is. Its biggest drawback is the public key of about 1.3 MB, while the ciphertext is tiny (240 bytes in this implementation). No practical attack is known. New cryptanalysis published in 2026 has, however, noticeably lowered its security estimates, and since October 2026 the German BSI advises against using Classic McEliece in new applications.
playground.step3DescFrodoKem: Lattice-based scheme that was an alternate candidate in round 3 of the NIST process and was not standardised by NIST. The German BSI recommends it nonetheless, and ISO standardisation is under way. As with ML-KEM, the client encapsulates a random secret under the server's public key. The difference is the foundation: FrodoKEM uses unstructured LWE instead of Module-LWE. Without the extra algebraic structure, attackers have less to work with, but the keys get large (public key about 21 KB). Like Classic McEliece 8192128, FrodoKEM-1344-AES reaches security category 5.
playground.step4Desc: HKDF-SHA256 derives a single 256-bit AES key from both shared secrets. To compute it, an attacker would have to break both X25519 and the chosen KEM.
playground.step5Desc: The combined key encrypts the message with AES-256-GCM, a scheme with built-in authentication. A random 12-byte IV makes sure the same message produces a different ciphertext every time.
playground.step6Desc: The recipient runs X25519 and KEM decapsulation, derives the same combinedKey and gets the original plaintext back.
playground.howToStep1: Client and server generate their key pairs independently: an X25519 pair for classical Diffie-Hellman and a KEM pair (ML-KEM, McEliece or FrodoKEM) for post-quantum security. Each private key stays with its owner.
playground.howToStep2: Client and server exchange their public X25519 keys and independently compute the same shared secret. This part is not quantum-safe, because a cryptographically relevant quantum computer could break X25519 with Shor's algorithm.
playground.howToStep3: The client encapsulates a random secret under the server's public KEM key (encapsulation), and the server recovers it with its private key (decapsulation). Both now hold the same KEM shared secret without it ever being transmitted.
playground.howToStep4: HKDF-SHA256 combines the X25519 shared secret and the KEM shared secret into one 256-bit AES key. Anyone who wants to compute it has to break both X25519 and the KEM.
playground.howToStep5: The combined key encrypts the plaintext with AES-256-GCM, an authenticated encryption scheme. A random 12-byte initialisation vector (IV) makes identical messages produce different ciphertexts.
playground.howToStep6: The recipient computes X25519 with their private key, decapsulates the KEM ciphertext, derives the same combinedKey via HKDF and decrypts the AES-GCM ciphertext. The result is the original plaintext.
playground.implArticleIntro: How this algorithm works internally is covered in
playground.mlkemImplProse: Pure TypeScript, no WASM. The library is kept small so you can review it yourself, but according to its own documentation it has not been independently audited yet. In the playground it runs in a Web Worker so the page stays responsive. One quirk when importing: the path needs the .js suffix, even in TypeScript projects. That applies to the whole @noble family and comes from ESM.
playground.mcElieceImplProse: The package contains the Classic McEliece C reference implementation, compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten. That explains the roughly 3 MB WASM bundle and the long keygen times. The API is async throughout because the WASM module initialises asynchronously. In the playground a Web Worker does the computing, so the tab stays usable even while McEliece keeps the worker busy for up to 30 seconds.
playground.frodoKemImplProse: @oqs/liboqs-js packages the liboqs C library from the Open Quantum Safe (OQS) project as WebAssembly. Few libraries cover as many PQC schemes as liboqs. The WASM is embedded as Base64 rather than shipped as a separate .wasm file, which keeps bundling simple. createFrodoKEM1344AES() loads and initialises the module asynchronously; after that, generateKeyPair() and encapsulate() run synchronously. Call kem.destroy() when you are done, otherwise the WASM memory is never released.
playground.step4QuantumNote: X25519 is broken, but the KEM share stays secret. So the combined key holds as well.
playground.mallorySummaryNeeds: To read the plaintext, she would need to:
playground.malloryCantBreakMlkem: ML-KEM: solve the Module-LWE problem (no efficient algorithm is known, quantum or classical)
playground.malloryCantBreakMceliece: Classic McEliece: decode a binary Goppa code without knowing its structure (no practical attack known, quantum or classical; security estimates did drop in 2026)
playground.malloryCantBreakFrodokem: FrodoKEM: solve the unstructured LWE problem (more conservative than Module-LWE, no known quantum attack)
playground.mallorySummaryQuantum: ⚡ With a quantum computer: X25519 is broken, but the KEM share stays secure. To get the combined HKDF key Mallory would need both parts, and one broken part is not enough.
playground.tamperHint: Click any public hex field and change one or more bytes. Then watch how the manipulation works its way through the protocol.
playground.tamperStep3WrongNote: ⚠ KEM ciphertext tampered → server decapsulates wrong secret
playground.tamperStep4WrongNote: ⚠ Wrong combined key — derived from incorrect KEM secret
playground.tamperStep6AesFail: The AES-GCM authentication tag does not match. The server notices the manipulation immediately: a single changed byte is enough to make the whole ciphertext useless.
playground.tamperStep6KemFail: The AES-GCM authentication tag does not match. The server derived a different combined key from the wrong KEM secret, so the tag does not fit.
playground.realWorldIntro: Hybrid post-quantum encryption is already in use and protects billions of connections today. Here are a few well-known examples; the list is far from complete.
playground.tooltipMean: The average of all 20 measurements. It is sensitive to outliers: a single very high value pulls the mean up, even if the other 19 measurements are close together.
playground.tooltipMedian: The middle value when all 20 measurements are sorted by size. Outliers barely affect it, so it often describes the typical runtime better than the mean.
playground.tooltipStd: The standard deviation tells you how far measurements deviate from the mean on average. Dividing by n−1 instead of n corrects the estimation bias of small samples, here 20 measurements.
playground.tooltipCV: Standard deviation divided by the mean, as a percentage. Below 10% the measurements are stable and reproducible. Above 30% points to strong fluctuations caused by the environment, such as browser scheduling or WASM initialisation.
playground.tooltipCI95: The true mean lies in this range with 95% probability. It is computed with the t-distribution (df = 19, t = 2.093), which is more accurate than the normal distribution for small samples. The narrower the interval, the more consistent the measurements.
playground.tooltipMinMax: The smallest and largest measured values from the 20 runs. Together with the IQR they show how widely the runtimes spread overall.
playground.tooltipIQR: The interquartile range covers the middle 50% of measurements, from the first quartile (25th percentile) to the third (75th percentile). A small IQR means most measurements are close together, no matter how extreme individual outliers are.
playground.tooltipOutliers: Measurements more than 1.5 times the IQR below Q1 or above Q3. They are statistically unusual and are often caused by the browser, for example by garbage collection or WASM loading.
playground.tooltipTrimmed: The mean without outliers. It shows the typical runtime more realistically than the raw mean, especially for schemes with a high CV such as Classic McEliece.
playground.benchmarkNote: Measured one after another (ML-KEM → FrodoKEM → McEliece) · 95%-CI: t-distribution df=19, t=2.093 · McEliece may take several minutes
playground.trackPqcDesc: Hybrid encryption and signatures with the new standards, step by step in your browser.
playground.trackPkiDesc: What does a post-quantum PKI look like? Larger demos, each with an article, that go beyond single algorithms.
playground.sigXmssLmsNote: // XMSS and LMS are missing because there are no usable JS packages for them: the XMSS package has not been updated since 2018, and there is none for LMS that runs in the browser. SLH-DSA covers the same use case, is also hash-based and is standardised by NIST.
playground.sigIntro: This playground shows digital signatures with classical and post-quantum schemes. Again, everything is computed in your browser. Pick an algorithm, enter a message and click "Sign". You will see key generation, signing and verification one after another. In tamper mode a single change is enough to make verification fail, and you can also switch on the attacker's or a quantum computer's view.
playground.sigStep1Desc: The signer generates a key pair of secret key and public key. The verifier receives the public key; the secret key stays with the signer.
playground.sigStep2DescEcdsa: The message is hashed with SHA-256 first. ECDSA then signs that hash with the private key. Its security rests on the discrete logarithm problem on elliptic curves.
playground.sigStep2DescMlDsa65: ML-DSA hashes the message internally with SHAKE-256 and computes the signature over module lattices (Module-LWE and Module-SIS). Rejection sampling ensures the signatures reveal nothing about the private key.
playground.sigStep2DescSlhDsa: SLH-DSA hashes internally with SHA-256 and builds the signature from a multi-layer hypertree made of one-time signatures (WOTS+) and a few-time signature scheme (FORS). There is no algebraic structure involved; security depends on the hash function alone.
playground.sigStep3DescEcdsa: The verifier computes SHA-256(message) on its own and then calls p256.verify(sig, SHA-256(msg), pk). The result is only valid if message, signature and public key all fit together.
playground.sigStep3Desc: The verifier passes signature, message and public key to verify(). The library hashes the message internally and checks whether the signature matches the public key. If it is valid, the message came from the signer and has not been changed.
playground.sigResultValid: ✓  Signature valid — content is authentic and unaltered
playground.sigResultInvalid: ✗  Signature invalid — content was altered or signature is forged
playground.sigTamperHint: Click the message or the signature and change it. Verification fails immediately.
playground.sigStep1QuantumBadgeEcdsa:
⚡ Shor can compute
SK from PK
playground.sigStep3QuantumWarningEcdsa: ⚡ With a quantum computer, ECDSA is broken: Shor's algorithm computes the secret key from the public key, and anyone can forge valid signatures.
playground.ecdsaImplProse: Pure JavaScript, no WASM. @noble/curves is a small library without external dependencies, audited by independent security firms. @noble/curves/nist.js contains P-256, P-384 and P-521. Watch out with p256.sign(): by default it expects a precomputed hash. With '{prehash: true}' it hashes the message with SHA-256 itself.
playground.mldsa65ImplProse: Pure TypeScript, no WASM. ML-DSA-65 is standardised in NIST FIPS 204 and derives from CRYSTALS-Dilithium. The library hashes the message internally with SHAKE-256 (FIPS 204, section 5.2), so you do not hash it yourself. Here too the import path needs the .js suffix, even in TypeScript projects.
playground.slhdsa128sImplProse: SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s (NIST FIPS 205) is a hash-based signature scheme. It needs neither lattices nor elliptic curves; the only assumption is that SHA-2 is secure. The 's' stands for 'small': tiny keys (32 and 64 bytes), but very slow signing (around 85 ms). Compared to SLH-DSA-SHA2-128f the signature is only about half the size (7,856 instead of 17,088 bytes), while signing takes roughly ten times as long. The package is loaded from @noble/post-quantum only when needed.
playground.slhdsa128fImplProse: SLH-DSA-SHA2-128f (NIST FIPS 205) is a hash-based signature scheme. The 'f' stands for 'fast': signing is quicker (around 8 ms), but at 17,088 bytes the signature is more than twice as large as with SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s, with identical keys. Comparing the two variants shows nicely how one scheme trades speed for size. The package is loaded from @noble/post-quantum only when needed.

playground.sigImplArticleComingSoonMlDsa65: // An article on how ML-DSA-65 works internally is in progress.
playground.sigImplArticleComingSoonSlhDsa128s: // An in-depth article on SLH-DSA is in progress.

playground.sigBenchmarkNote: Measured sequentially (ECDSA → ML-DSA → SLH-DSA-128f → SLH-DSA-128s) · 95% CI: t-distribution, df=19, t=2.093 · SLH-DSA-128s may take several seconds
playground.sigRealWorldIntro: Signatures sit in every HTTPS connection, every software update and every signed document. The switch to post-quantum schemes has started.
playground.step3EncapNote: // internally: fresh random bytes, ephemeral — unique to this session
playground.step3EncapSent: // ciphertext → transmitted to server (visible on the wire)
playground.step3DecapEphNote: sk_server is ephemeral — discarded after this step
playground.step3PfsText: Both sides use ephemeral keys that are generated fresh for each session and discarded right afterwards. Someone who keeps a full recording of this session and later gets hold of every key still cannot decrypt it, because the ephemeral keys no longer exist.
playground.step3PfsX25519: X25519: client generates an ephemeral key pair → private key deleted immediately after the DH step
playground.step3PfsKem: KEM: server generates an ephemeral KEM key pair → private key deleted immediately after decapsulation
playground.step3PfsCombined: The two parts are independent. An attacker would have to break both while the session is running; afterwards it is too late.
playground.step3PfsMcElieceIntro: Classic McEliece key generation takes 10 to 30 seconds. Generating a fresh KEM key for every session is therefore not realistic, and in production the server key is usually static.
playground.step3PfsMcElieceKemWarn: KEM (McEliece) static: someone who keeps the recording and later obtains the private KEM key can reconstruct kemSS. On the KEM side there is no forward secrecy.
playground.step3PfsMcElieceX25519: X25519: the client's key pair is ephemeral, and its private key is gone for good after the DH step. X25519 therefore provides forward secrecy in any case.
playground.step3PfsMcElieceCombined: The hybrid keeps forward secrecy because HKDF needs both x25519SS and kemSS. Knowing only kemSS, for example after the static key has been stolen, is not enough to compute the session key, since x25519SS no longer exists.
playground.step3PfsMcElieceDemoNote: In this demo the McEliece keys are regenerated for every session. Production systems usually do not do that.

pkiPlayground.label: // pki playground
pkiPlayground.title: What does a post-quantum PKI look like?
pkiPlayground.intro: New algorithms alone do not make a post-quantum infrastructure. Certificates, chains of trust and key distribution have to follow, and some weaknesses of today's PKI can be solved in a fundamentally different way with lattice-based schemes. Every demo comes with an article that explains the background.

rbe.title: Registration-Based Encryption
rbe.desc: Encrypt to an identity as in identity-based encryption, but without any party that knows all private keys. Everyone generates their own key pair, and a key curator with no secret combines the public keys into a single master key. The demo implements the paper's base construction with three people.

cbom.metaDescription: Cryptography inventory of beyond-shor.eu: {count} assets across {libs} libraries, scanned with ShorSight, published as a signed CycloneDX CBOM with a risk analysis following BSI Standard 200-3.
cbom.intro: What cryptography does beyond-shor.eu use, and where? The answer comes from ShorSight, a cryptography inventory tool. It analyses source code semantically rather than by pattern matching, backs every finding with a file and line, and assesses it twice: against classical attacks and against quantum computers. In this website it found {count} cryptographic assets across {libs} libraries.
cbom.embedNote: Below is ShorSight’s own interface, reduced to the inventory and risk management views.
cbom.scopeNote: What is inventoried is what does cryptographic work in this repository. The hosting provider’s TLS layer, Node’s internal hashes for package integrity and build tooling are deliberately out of scope.
cbom.embedTitle: ShorSight: cryptography inventory and risk management of beyond-shor.eu
cbom.downloadNote: CycloneDX {spec}, signed with ML-DSA-65, verifiable in your browser
cbom.evidenceInfo:
How the asset was identified.

literal: an exact crypto API or constant found in the code — the strongest evidence.

resolved: inferred from imports or usage.

name-only: matched by name alone — the weakest.
cbom.libIntro: Version marker: 📌 = exact version resolved from a lockfile, so CVEs are matched precisely. ~ = a manifest range only, so the installed version is not pinned and CVE matching is left unknown. No marker = no version found, e.g. a stdlib module.
cbom.transitiveTitle: pulled in indirectly through another dependency
cbom.versionUnpinnedTitle: from a manifest range, not pinned
cbom.cveUnknownTitle: version not pinned (no lockfile) — CVE matching is not possible
cbom.sinksInfo:
The places where this code sends data across a network boundary or takes it in.

These are not weaknesses. The list shows where transport security has to hold and where a cryptographic asset sits on such a boundary.
cbom.sinkCryptoAsset: cryptographic asset at a network boundary
cbom.riskIntro: The risk analysis is modelled on BSI Standard 200-3, with Mosca’s rule as the engine of urgency. The impact of each object (algorithm × asset) is derived from human-set security objectives and the economic damage per asset; the urgency from the classical status (acute) or from Mosca (quantum). Two matrices keep the regimes apart. This page shows a completed assessment — it is edited in ShorSight, not here.
cbom.riskInfoAcute:
Broken or weak with today’s computers, or carrying a CVE in its library.

Act on these now, independently of any quantum concern.
cbom.riskInfoQuantum:
Secure today, but breakable by a future quantum computer (Shor).

The urgency follows Mosca’s rule X + Y > Z. Confidentiality is judged against the assumed CRQC year {crqc} — an attacker can harvest now and decrypt later — and signatures against {sig}.
cbom.riskInfoNone:
Quantum-safe and classically secure.

No action is needed.
cbom.riskInfoCrqc:
The assumed number of years until a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) exists.

Confidentiality uses the BSI estimate of about {crqc}.

Signatures use the more aggressive Google and Cloudflare projection of about {sig}.

Source: Cloudflare post-quantum roadmap.
cbom.matrixNoteQuantum: Classically secure but quantum-unsafe or unknown.
cbom.matrixNoteAcute: Broken or weak today, or a CVE in the library.
cbom.matrixInfoQuantum:
How an object lands in this matrix.

Impact axis (1–4) — for every object it is max( the asset’s role-relevant security objectives , its economic damage ). A signature uses integrity, authenticity and non-repudiation, encryption uses confidentiality; the economic damage always applies. Until an asset is fully assessed the impact stays provisional and is derived from its criticality.

Urgency axis (1–4) — Mosca’s X + Y > Z: X = data shelf-life, Y = migration time, Z = the assumed CRQC year. Bands: 4 overdue (X+Y is already past Z), 3 urgent (two years of head-room at most), 2 mid-term (five at most), 1 watch (more). Signatures ignore X — there is no retroactive forgery — and race the earlier signature CRQC year.

Cell = risk — the BSI 200-3 lookup of impact × urgency, coloured low to very high.
cbom.matrixInfoAcute:
How an object lands in this matrix.

Impact axis (1–4) — for every object it is max( the asset’s role-relevant security objectives , its economic damage ), set in the impact assessment below.

Urgency axis (1–4) — classical exploitability today: the worse of the algorithm’s status (broken → 4, weak → 3) and its library’s CVE severity (critical → 4, high → 3, medium → 2, low → 1). Mosca’s X, Y and Z play no role here.

Cell = risk — the BSI 200-3 lookup of impact × urgency.
cbom.impactIntro: Per source: four security objectives (1–4) and the economic damage on failure. An object’s impact is max( role-relevant objectives , economic damage ). Assets that are not fully assessed fall back provisionally to their criticality. These values are a human judgement — no scanner can derive them.
cbom.needsInputTitle: security objectives and economic damage are not fully set
cbom.anchorsEconLead: Economic damage if the asset fails:
cbom.treatmentIntro: One decision per object, owned by the risk owner. At impact 4 (existential) transfer and accept are barred — only avoid or reduce remain.
cbom.impactInfo:
Impact (1–4) = max( the asset’s role-relevant security objectives , its economic damage ), set in the impact assessment.

A signature inherits integrity, authenticity and non-repudiation; encryption inherits confidentiality; economic damage always applies as a floor.

~ marks a provisional value derived from criticality while the asset is not fully assessed.
cbom.treatmentInfo:
The risk-treatment decision under BSI 200-3: Avoid (remove the risk), Reduce (mitigate, e.g. migrate to PQC), Transfer (shift to a third party), Accept (consciously bear it).

At impact 4, transfer and accept are barred.
cbom.vendorDepTitle: vendor-dependent: the migration is not in your own hands
cbom.findingsInfo:
Each finding is sorted with Mosca’s rule X + Y > Z.

ACUTE: broken or weak today, or a CVE in the library.

QUANTUM!: quantum-breakable and urgent.

quantum: quantum-breakable, not yet urgent.
cbom.migrationInfo:
Manually maintained migration status (MV-CBOM): not started, planned, in progress, hybrid, PQC only, not applicable.

The deadline is the year by which the migration must be complete according to the Mosca analysis.
cbom.findingSummaryAcute: Attackable with today’s means. Deal with it regardless of any quantum concern.
cbom.findingSummaryQuantum: Secure today, but a future quantum computer breaks it with Shor’s algorithm.
cbom.moscaRelaxed: Protects data ~{x}y; migration ~{y}y against ~{z}y until {crqc}. {x}+{y}={sum} ≤ {z} → there is time; plan the migration (start by {startBy}).
cbom.moscaUrgent: Protects data ~{x}y; migration ~{y}y against ~{z}y until {crqc}. {x}+{y}={sum} > {z} → harvest now, decrypt later; migrate now.
cbom.registerIntro: Sorted by urgency, then by business criticality.

rationale.aes-256-gcm: Authenticated encryption; the 256-bit key keeps at least 128-bit security under Grover.
rationale.aes-gcm: AES-GCM authenticated encryption; the key size (128/192/256) is not statically determinable.
rationale.classic-mceliece: Code-based post-quantum KEM with very large public keys; since October 2026 the BSI advises against new deployments.
rationale.ec-p256: NIST P-256 elliptic curve (the use was not inferred from a bare curve constant); broken by Shor’s algorithm.
rationale.frodokem-1344-aes: Conservative lattice-based (LWE) post-quantum KEM, 1344 parameter set with AES as the internal PRF; NIST level 5.
rationale.hkdf: HMAC-based key derivation (RFC 5869); sound for deriving keys from high-entropy input.
rationale.hmac: Security depends on the underlying hash; safe with SHA-2 or SHA-3.
rationale.ml-kem-1024: NIST FIPS 203 post-quantum KEM (CRYSTALS-Kyber), security level 5.
rationale.sha-256: SHA-2; Grover only reduces preimage security to 2^128, which remains safe.
rationale.slh-dsa-sha2-128f: NIST FIPS 205 SLH-DSA-SHA2-128f (SPHINCS+): fast signing, larger signatures; NIST level 1.
rationale.slh-dsa-sha2-128s: NIST FIPS 205 SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s (SPHINCS+): small signatures, slow signing; NIST level 1.
rationale.x25519: Curve25519 key agreement; broken by Shor.
rationale.shake256: Keccak extendable-output function (SHA-3 family); Grover reduces the security level, which remains sufficient.

treatmentNote.x25519: Deliberate: X25519 is the classical half of the hybrid handshake and is paired with ML-KEM-1024.
treatmentNote.ec-p256: ECDSA P-256 is kept as the classical reference point in the signature benchmark.

rbe.metaDescription: Interactive demo of Registration-Based Encryption (RBE): lattice-based, without key escrow, with a key curator that knows no secret.
rbe.intro: This demo implements Registration-Based Encryption (RBE) following the base construction by Zhang, Ding, Malavolta and Döttling. A key curator with no secret manages the public keys, and everything the users do runs in your browser.
rbe.paramsSubtitle: The demo follows the construction from the paper exactly, but with smaller parameters so that it runs in milliseconds in the browser. The table compares the two.
rbe.param_construction_explain: The compact variant shrinks the ciphertext by roughly a factor of l, but needs a structured CRS with a Gaussian trapdoor. In the paper its setup takes about 40 minutes.
rbe.param_q_explain: The modulus determines how much noise decryption tolerates. At 26 bits every product stays below 2⁵³, so the browser computes exactly without BigInt.
rbe.param_nR_explain: Degree of the ring R_q = Z_q[X]/(X^n_R + 1). At 256 the noise stays at least eleven standard deviations below the limit q/4 in every measured session with 26 bits. At 512 the margin depends heavily on the keys and drops to about three standard deviations in unlucky sessions, where individual decryptions fail. 1024 would need a larger modulus.
rbe.param_n_explain: Rows of the CRS blocks. A higher rank increases security, but also noise and data size.
rbe.param_d_explain: Base of the decomposition G⁻¹. A larger base means fewer digits and smaller ciphertexts, but faster noise growth. m is the width of one CRS block.
rbe.param_l_explain: Every identity bit costs one CRS block and adds m ring elements to ct0.
rbe.param_N_explain: Registered users. A registration always costs the same, computing a helper key grows linearly with the number of users.
rbe.param_ct_explain: Most of it is ct0 with (l + 1) · m ring elements.
rbe.securityNote: The construction works exactly as in the paper, but the parameters are heavily reduced. Among other things, the security proof needs a much larger modulus (for noise smudging) and longer identities. This demo therefore makes no security claim and is not meant for production use.
rbe.impl1: It implements the base construction from Section 3. The CRS is a uniform matrix without a trapdoor, and the key curator holds no secret.
rbe.impl2: The CRS is expanded from a public seed with SHAKE-256. Identities are {l} bits taken from SHAKE-256 of the name.
rbe.impl3: The NOT gate inside the delta function is evaluated linearly (A_l − A_k) instead of multiplicatively as in Algorithms 3 to 5. Both satisfy the same equation from Theorem 4, but the linear version gives much shorter helper keys. That is what makes a 26-bit modulus sufficient.
rbe.impl4: In Algorithm 4 (line 9) and Algorithm 5 (line 11) of the paper the condition is flipped: it has to be (1 − i_k) instead of i_k. Implemented literally, Algorithm 4 satisfies Theorem 4 for none of 64 tested identity pairs; corrected, for all of them.
rbe.impl5: The chains for A_δi are precomputed once at registration (cf. the preprocessing in Section 5.1). A helper key is then just a sum of precomputed blocks.
rbe.impl6: Automated tests check the equations exactly: Theorem 4 for all identity pairs, (A − ĩ ⊗ G) · hsk_i = mpk − pk_i for every user, and a noise margin of at least six standard deviations.

rbePlayground.introComment: // what is rbe, and why does it need no certificate?
rbePlayground.intro1: In a classical PKI, Alice has her public key signed by a certificate authority, and anyone who wants to write to her checks that certificate. With identity-based encryption (IBE) her name is enough, but the central authority knows every secret key. That is called key escrow.
rbePlayground.intro2: Registration-Based Encryption (RBE) combines the two: everyone generates their own key pair and only registers the public key with the key curator (KC). The KC compresses all public keys into one compact mpk. To encrypt, you only need mpk and the recipient's name.
rbePlayground.intro3: The KC holds no secret. Everything it computes can be recomputed by anyone from public data. This demo implements the base construction from Section 3 of the paper: what the users do runs in your browser, the KC runs on the server, and in step 3 your browser audits it.
rbePlayground.step0Title: Setup: a public CRS with no backdoor
rbePlayground.step0Text: The KC publishes a random seed. SHAKE-256 expands it into the common reference string <c>A = [A_0 | … | A_l]</c>: {blocks} uniform blocks over the ring <c>R_q</c>, one per identity bit and one for the constant 1. Because A is derived from the seed alone, anyone can check that it hides no structure.
rbePlayground.step0Expanded: A expanded from the seed in {ms} ms · first coefficients of A_0
rbePlayground.step0Callout: How can this be secure if everything is public? Security does not rest on a secret held by the KC, but on the users' secret keys and the LWE problem. The KC only manages public data and does the computation for everyone else.
rbePlayground.step13Text1: Everyone generates their key pair locally, here in the browser. The secret key is a short vector <c>sk = (−s, 1)</c>, the public key an LWE instance <c>pk = (B | B·s + e)</c> with a small error <c>e</c>. So <c>pk · sk = e ≈ 0</c>, yet s cannot be computed from pk.
rbePlayground.step13Text2: The identity is an {ell}-bit number, here taken from SHAKE-256 of the name. On registration the KC computes the contribution <c>A_δi · G⁻¹(pk_i)</c> and adds it to <c>mpk</c>. <c>A_δi</c> is the homomorphic evaluation of the function "equals i" on the CRS, and <c>G⁻¹</c> splits every coefficient into base-{d} digits.
rbePlayground.step13Done: N_max = {max} reached. The KC has combined three public keys into a single mpk of {k} ring elements without seeing a single secret.
rbePlayground.auditMatch: It matches. From the seed and the three public keys your browser computed exactly the same mpk as the KC, in {ms} ms. That is how any key curator can be audited.
rbePlayground.auditMismatch: Mismatch! The KC's mpk does not fit the registered public keys.
rbePlayground.step4Title: Encryption: Charlie writes to Bob and Alice
rbePlayground.step4Text: Charlie only needs public data: the CRS, mpk and the recipient's identity. The identity sits in <c>ct0</c>, because Charlie encrypts under <c>A − ĩ ⊗ G</c>, a CRS with the identity bits built in. <c>ct1</c> carries the message, one bit per coefficient at distance ⌊q/2⌋. Fresh small random values <c>r</c>, <c>e0</c> and <c>e1</c> are added.
rbePlayground.ctSummary: ct0: {ct0} ring elements · ct1: {ct1} · together ≈ {kib} KiB · in {ms} ms
rbePlayground.step4Obs: Observation: the two ciphertexts differ in the identity built into them, {bob}₂ for Bob and {alice}₂ for Alice. That is exactly what stops Alice from reading Bob's message in step 6.
rbePlayground.step5Title: Decryption: helper key and secret key
rbePlayground.step5Text: To decrypt, the recipient fetches her helper key <c>hsk</c> from the KC. The KC computes it from public data too, namely from all registered public keys. It satisfies <c>(A − ĩ ⊗ G) · hsk_i = mpk − pk_i</c> and is short: its coefficients are much smaller than q.
rbePlayground.decStep1Text: Step 1 (public): ct1 − ct0 · hsk removes the share of all other users. What remains is an ordinary dual-Regev encryption under the recipient's own public key: r · pk_i + message + noise.
rbePlayground.decStep1Result: dual-Regev ciphertext under pk_{name}, not readable yet
rbePlayground.decStep2Text: Step 2 (secret): multiplying by sk leaves only r · e + message + noise. Every coefficient is then close to 0 or to q/2 and gets rounded.
rbePlayground.noiseLabel: noise: at most {pct} % of the tolerance q/4
rbePlayground.step5Done: Two factors: hsk is public and useless on its own, sk never leaves the browser. The KC cannot decrypt anything because it has no sk, and neither can anyone who only intercepts hsk. There is no key escrow.
rbePlayground.step6Title: Cross-check: Alice tries to read Bob's message
rbePlayground.step6Text1: Alice is registered, has her own helper key and has just decrypted her message. Now she applies <c>hsk_alice</c> and <c>sk_alice</c> to Bob's ciphertext.
rbePlayground.step6Text2: That cannot work. hsk_alice satisfies the equation for Alice's identity only. On Bob's ct0, step 1 leaves a residual term <c>r · ((ĩ_alice − ĩ_bob) ⊗ G) · hsk_alice</c>, and its coefficients are large and practically random.
rbePlayground.btnAttack: Apply hsk_alice and sk_alice to Bob's ciphertext
rbePlayground.step6Done: The identity binding holds. Alice can read her own messages but not Bob's. Her noise is close to 100 % of the tolerance: the coefficients are practically uniform, and rounding produces only randomness.
